title: Spine-containing unions of consecutive interval faces are Segal-local equivalences
statement:
Use the small simplicial spaces, representables $F(m)$, mapping simplicial sets $\operatorname{Map}$ and Reedy model structure of [lem-coef-simplicial-space-reedy-cartesian]. For $m\geq1$, let $G(m)\subseteq F(m)$ be the union of all consecutive edges, with $G(1)=F(1)$. For integers $0\leq a<b\leq m$, let $F([a,b])\subseteq F(m)$ be the image of $F(b-a)$ under the injection $j\mapsto a+j$ for $0\leq j\leq b-a$. Let $\mathcal I$ be a finite collection of such intervals and put $H=\bigcup_{[a,b]\in\mathcal I}F([a,b])$. Assume $G(m)\subseteq H$. Let $V$ be a small Reedy fibrant simplicial space such that, for every $r\geq2$, its consecutive-edge comparison $V_r\to V_1\times_{V_0}\cdots\times_{V_0}V_1$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. Then restriction induces a weak homotopy equivalence
$$\operatorname{Map}(F(m),V)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}(H,V).$$

source.place: Rezk, A model for the homotopy theory of homotopy theory, Lemma 10.1, printed p. 23: precise spine-containing interval-union version used in the proof of Lemma 10.3. The spine-containment hypothesis replaces the insufficient all-vertices condition in the online text; see report.md Source error. Read online, not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this simplicial-space result.

proof.text: For every inclusion $A\subseteq B$ of small simplicial spaces, the monomorphism/cofibration clause and the mapping-space clause of [lem-coef-simplicial-space-reedy-cartesian], applied to the Reedy fibration $V\to *$, give a Kan fibration $\operatorname{Map}(B,V)\to\operatorname{Map}(A,V)$. Here $\operatorname{Map}(A,*)=\operatorname{Map}(B,*)=*$ directly from the definition. In particular all these mapping spaces are Kan, by taking $A=\varnothing$. By the Kan model structure of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper] and the meaning of trivial in [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure], a restriction which is also a weak homotopy equivalence is a trivial Kan fibration.

source.place: Sections 2.3-2.5, printed pp. 5-7; mapping-space axiom used in Lemma 10.1.

proof.text:
We will use two explicit closure calculations. If $p:E\to B$ is a trivial Kan fibration, it lifts against every $\partial\Delta^q\hookrightarrow\Delta^q$, including $q=0$, by [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. A square against its pullback $T\times_BE\to T$ projects to a square against $p$; a filler $e:\Delta^q\to E$ pairs with the prescribed map $t:\Delta^q\to T$ to give the filler $(t,e)$ in the pullback. Thus pullbacks are trivial Kan fibrations by the same boundary-lifting criterion. For a composite $E\xrightarrow{p}B\xrightarrow{q}C$ of trivial Kan fibrations, first fill a boundary square against $q$ with boundary map obtained by applying $p$, then fill against $p$ over this chosen simplex of $B$. Hence finite composites, including the identity, are trivial Kan fibrations. Also, if $U=A\cup_KB$ is the union of two subobjects with intersection $K$, then
$$\operatorname{Map}(U,V)=\operatorname{Map}(A,V)\times_{\operatorname{Map}(K,V)}\operatorname{Map}(B,V).$$
Indeed in each inner degree $q$, a map $U\times c\Delta^q\to V$ is exactly a pair of maps from $A\times c\Delta^q$ and $B\times c\Delta^q$ agreeing on $K\times c\Delta^q$. The union and intersection assertions hold in each bidegree, and all operators preserve them, so these bijections commute with the inner simplicial operators. This uses the mapping-space definition in [lem-coef-simplicial-space-reedy-cartesian].

source.place: Lemma 10.1, printed p. 23: expansion of the passage from unions of interval faces to mapping spaces, using the Section 2.3 mapping-space formula.

proof.text: Evaluation at $1_{[r]}$ identifies $\operatorname{Map}(F(r),V)$ with $V_r$ as simplicial sets. Explicitly, a $q$-simplex $v\in V_{r,q}$ gives the map $F(r)\times c\Delta^q\to V$ whose value on $(\alpha:[k]\to[r],\beta:[s]\to[q])$ is $V(\alpha,\beta)(v)$; evaluating at $(1_{[r]},1_{[q]})$ gives the inverse. Naturality proves both inverse identities. The consecutive edges of $G(r)$ form a chain of copies of $F(1)$, meeting adjacent copies in their common endpoint $F(0)$ and nonadjacent copies in the empty subobject. Thus the degreewise gluing calculation of step 2 identifies $\operatorname{Map}(G(r),V)$ with the iterated fibre product of $r$ copies of $V_1$ over $V_0$, using the target of one edge and the source of the next. Under these identifications, restriction is exactly the consecutive-edge comparison in the hypothesis, so it is a weak homotopy equivalence for $r\geq2$. For $r=1$ it is the identity since $G(1)=F(1)$. In every case it is also a Kan fibration by step 1, hence a trivial Kan fibration. The representables and mapping formula used here are those of [lem-coef-simplicial-space-reedy-cartesian].

source.place: Section 4.1 and Lemma 10.1, printed pp. 11 and 23: the spine comparison, expanded by evaluation and degreewise gluing.

proof.text: Prove the stated conclusion by strong induction on $m\geq1$, for the fixed $V$ and all interval collections in $F(m)$. If $m=1$, spine containment forces $H=F(1)$, giving an identity. At an inductive stage $m>1$, the case $H=F(m)$ is likewise an identity. Otherwise each interval $I=[a,b]$ in $\mathcal I$ has length $\ell=b-a<m$, because the only interval of length $m$ is $[0,m]$. Enumerate the finite collection as $I_1,\ldots,I_N$, and put $H_0=G(m)$ and $H_j=G(m)\cup\bigcup_{i\leq j}F(I_i)$. Spine containment gives $H_N=H$. For $I_j=[a,b]$ put $K_j=H_{j-1}\cap F(I_j)$. Then $K_j$ is a finite union of consecutive interval faces in $F(I_j)\cong F(\ell_j)$ and contains its entire spine. To check this, a simplex of $F([a,b])$ is a monotone map whose image lies in $[a,b]$. Hence $F([a,b])\cap F([c,d])$ is empty if $\max(a,c)>\min(b,d)$, and otherwise is the full face on $[\max(a,c),\min(b,d)]$. The intersection $G(m)\cap F([a,b])$ is exactly the spine on $[a,b]$: edges wholly in the interval give its consecutive edges; any endpoint contributed by an edge outside the interval already belongs to that spine since $a<b$. Any singleton interval arising from an intersection is likewise already in the spine and may be discarded. Translating indices by $a$ therefore expresses $K_j$ using intervals with distinct endpoints in $[0,\ell_j]$, exactly as required by the induction hypothesis.

source.place: Lemma 10.1, printed p. 23: the interval-intersection argument, expanded as strong induction on ambient simplex length.

proof.text: For each $j$, apply the induction hypothesis at $1\leq\ell_j<m$ to the interval union $K_j\subseteq F(I_j)\cong F(\ell_j)$ from step 4. The same Reedy fibrant $V$ satisfies every Segal comparison needed there, so $\operatorname{Map}(F(I_j),V)\to\operatorname{Map}(K_j,V)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. It is also a Kan fibration by step 1 and is therefore trivial. The union square $H_j=H_{j-1}\cup_{K_j}F(I_j)$ and step 2 identify $\operatorname{Map}(H_j,V)\to\operatorname{Map}(H_{j-1},V)$ with its pullback along $\operatorname{Map}(H_{j-1},V)\to\operatorname{Map}(K_j,V)$. The boundary-filler calculation of step 2 makes this restriction a trivial Kan fibration. Composing for $j=1,\ldots,N$ gives a trivial Kan fibration $\operatorname{Map}(H,V)\to\operatorname{Map}(G(m),V)$. The ingredients used are the mapping-space fibration clause of [lem-coef-simplicial-space-reedy-cartesian] and the trivial-Kan-fibration characterization of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]; the only inductive application has strictly smaller ambient length, so no assertion at $m$ is assumed.

source.place: Lemma 10.1, printed p. 23: finite gluing of interval faces; explicit trivial-fibration pullback argument replaces an unstated homotopy-colimit assertion.

proof.text:
The composite
$$\operatorname{Map}(F(m),V)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}(H,V)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}(G(m),V)$$
is the spine restriction, a weak homotopy equivalence by step 3. Its second factor is a weak homotopy equivalence by step 5. Apply the two-out-of-three axiom in [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure] to the Kan model structure of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. The first factor is a weak homotopy equivalence, which proves the induction claim and the item. All arrows are the specified restriction maps because their composites precompose with the composed inclusions.

source.place: Lemma 10.1, printed p. 23: final two-out-of-three argument.
